record.paper_title: Open Problems on Information and Feedback Controlled Systems
record.original_question: How can the thermodynamics of feedback-controlled systems be formulated so that the thermodynamic effects of information transfer between the system and the controller are explicitly accounted for? The formulation should support thermodynamic quantities and limits such as maximum efficiency and bounds on work that can be extracted from the feedback-controlled system.

evidence.quote: The second main question is the establishment of the thermodynamics of feedback controlled systems accounting for thermodynamic effects of the information transfer.
the computation of the maximum efficiency involves a bound in the work that can be extracted from the feedback controlled system

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Develop a thermodynamic framework for feedback-controlled physical systems in which the thermodynamic effects of the information transfer between the controlled system and its controller are explicitly accounted for. More precisely:

(a) Consider a physical system S coupled to one or several heat reservoirs and to an external controller C. The controller performs measurements on S (acquiring information described by a mutual information I(S;C)) and, based on the measurement outcomes, applies a feedback protocol that drives S. Define, within this setup, thermodynamic quantities (entropy production, heat, work, and free energy changes) that consistently incorporate the information acquired and/or used by the controller.

(b) Using this framework, derive a refinement of the second law of thermodynamics for feedback-controlled systems that gives a tight upper bound on the work W that can be extracted from S in terms of the free-energy change of S and the information-theoretic quantities characterizing the measurement-feedback loop.

(c) Define a notion of efficiency for such feedback-controlled engines and compute its maximum value as a function of the information transferred between S and C, exhibiting protocols that saturate the bound.

The framework should reduce to ordinary stochastic thermodynamics in the limit of no measurement (zero information transfer), and should apply to both discrete (single measurement and feedback step) and continuous (continuous information flow) feedback schemes.
artifact.status_search_result: Significant progress has been made: Sagawa–Ueda-type generalized second laws, Cao–Feito's "Thermodynamics of feedback controlled systems" (Phys. Rev. E 79, 041118, 2009), and Horowitz–Esposito's "Thermodynamics with Continuous Information Flow" (Phys. Rev. X 4, 031015, 2014) provide frameworks in which work extraction is bounded by mutual information. More recent works (e.g., 2024 papers on finite-time bounds and optimal work extraction with imprecise measurements) continue to refine efficiency bounds. While the basic formulation is widely regarded as solved for broad classes of systems, the program of fully characterizing maximum efficiency and tight work bounds in general (e.g., finite-time, non-Markovian, delayed feedback) remains active, so the overall problem is best classified as partially solved.

status_evidence.title: Thermodynamics of feedback controlled systems
status_evidence.snippet: A refinement of the second law for feedback systems establishes a bound to the extracted energy, met by optimal feedback engines.
status_evidence.claim: Established a bound on work extracted from feedback-controlled systems via a refined second law.

status_evidence.title: Thermodynamics with Continuous Information Flow
status_evidence.snippet: Framework extending stochastic thermodynamics to systems with continuous information flow between subsystems.
status_evidence.claim: Provides a thermodynamic formalism that explicitly accounts for information transfer in feedback loops.

status_evidence.title: Finite-time thermodynamic bounds and tradeoff relations for information processing
status_evidence.snippet: Tradeoff relations between dissipation from measurement and feedback in information processing.
status_evidence.claim: Active recent work refining efficiency bounds, indicating the problem is not fully closed.
